planting.note: Direct sow in early spring through late spring, or in fall for a cool-season crop; Muir is notably heat- and bolt-tolerant for a loose-leaf lettuce, extending the harvest window later into warm weather than most leaf types.

directions: Sow directly 1/4 inch deep in fertile, moisture-retentive soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; thin to 6–10 inches and harvest as cut-and-come-again or as full heads. Muir is a French heirloom oakleaf-type loose-leaf lettuce developed as a heat-tolerant selection, producing a loose, upright rosette of thick, savoyed, chartreuse-green leaves with a distinctively crisp, succulent texture and mild, sweet flavor that holds up better than most leaf lettuces once temperatures start climbing. Its unusually thick, crinkled leaf texture also makes it more forgiving of the wilting summer sun than thinner-leafed varieties, and it is slower to turn bitter as it approaches bolting. A useful bridge variety for gardeners who want fresh salad greens into the early part of a Gulf South summer before switching to heat-adapted greens, in zone 3–10.
sources: Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners

planting.note: Plant dormant bushes fall through early spring in cool-summer climates in fertile, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; gooseberries perform poorly in hot, humid summer climates and need afternoon shade and reliable soil moisture where summers are warm.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun where summers are cool; mulch to keep roots cool and moist, and prune to an open framework each winter to ease harvest among the thorny stems. Hinnomaki Red is a Finnish-bred gooseberry cultivar prized for combining reliable productivity, good mildew resistance, and outstanding fruit quality — the medium-sized berries ripen from green to a deep red-burgundy with a rich, sweet-tart flavor considered among the best of any gooseberry for fresh eating out of hand, as well as excellent for pies, jams, and fools. The compact, upright bush is more manageable and less sprawling than many older gooseberry varieties, and its Nordic breeding gives it strong cold hardiness alongside dependable disease resistance in cool, humid summer climates. Best suited to northern gardens with cool summers; in hot, humid zones the plant struggles with heat stress and powdery mildew regardless of afternoon shade. Zone 3–7.
sources: Cornell University Small Fruit Production Guide

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in late winter to early spring; in zone 8–9 plant December–February for best establishment before summer heat. Powderblue blooms late-mid season and cross-pollinates best with Brightwell, Tifblue, or Climax — plant at least two varieties within 50 feet for maximum fruit set.

directions: Plant in acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), well-drained, sandy or loamy soil amended with pine bark or peat in full sun; Powderblue is a University of Georgia-released rabbiteye blueberry valued for its vigorous, upright, disease-resistant growth habit and dependable, heavy production of firm, small-to-medium, powder-blue berries with excellent shelf life and a mild, sweet flavor well suited to both fresh eating and freezing. It ripens mid-to-late season, several weeks after Climax and Premier, helping extend the rabbiteye harvest window into July in most Gulf Coast plantings. The upright, vigorous canes tend to sucker less than some rabbiteye varieties, keeping the planting tidier, and the bush shows good tolerance of the humid, disease-prone conditions typical of southeastern summers. Mulch heavily with pine bark, maintain consistent moisture through fruit development, and fertilize with an acid-forming fertilizer at bloom and again after harvest. Zone 6–9.
sources: University of Georgia Extension — Rabbiteye Blueberry Varieties
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Rabbiteye Blueberry Production
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Blueberry Production in Louisiana

planting.note: Plant dormant canes in late winter through early spring; in zone 8–9 plant February–March for maximum establishment. Choctaw is a thorny, erect variety that fruits early, typically late May to early June in the Gulf South — among the earliest-ripening named blackberries.

directions: Plant dormant canes 1–2 inches deep in fertile, well-drained, acidic soil; Choctaw is an erect, thorny blackberry developed by the University of Arkansas breeding program and released in 1980, one of the earliest-ripening blackberry varieties available and long valued in the mid-South and Gulf Coast for extending the harvest season ahead of later thornless varieties. The medium-sized berries are glossy black, firm, and exceptionally sweet with small seeds and outstanding flavor, considered by many Southern growers among the best-tasting of the University of Arkansas blackberry releases even decades after its introduction. The erect canes are self-supporting and highly productive, though the thorns require more careful handling at harvest and pruning than newer thornless varieties. Prune floricanes to the ground immediately after harvest; tip primocanes at about 36 inches in summer to encourage the lateral branches that carry the following year's crop. An excellent early-season partner for later-ripening varieties like Ouachita or Natchez to extend the blackberry harvest across the whole season. Zone 6–9.
sources: University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Blackberry Variety Selection
LSU AgCenter Publication #2207 — Blackberry and Raspberry Production
